option_description: Controls whether the kube-apiserver accepts unauthenticated requests, processing them under the system:anonymous identity. When true (or flag absent), any network-reachable client can interact with the API server without presenting credentials.
security_impact: Two Rego conditions fire when this is true: (1) anonymous_auth_enabled=true AND no network_policy_restricts_api_server_egress triggers api_server_unauthenticated_ingress_exposure; (2) anonymous_auth_enabled=true AND no api_server_firewall_ingress_restricted also triggers the same exposure. Essentially, anonymous auth creates an unauthenticated ingress surface that bypasses the first authentication layer of the control plane boundary, allowing attackers to enumerate API endpoints, probe RBAC gaps, and exploit any publicly exposed cluster endpoint without credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the kube-apiserver static pod manifest on the control plane node for the --anonymous-auth flag value.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'anonymous-auth' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Should show '- --anonymous-auth=false'. If the flag is absent or shows '=true', anonymous auth is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the running kube-apiserver process arguments directly on the control plane node to confirm the active flag, independent of the manifest.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o 'anonymous-auth=[^ ]*'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns 'anonymous-auth=false' if properly disabled. No output or 'anonymous-auth=true' indicates anonymous auth is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Probe the API server from a node or pod to verify whether anonymous requests are accepted by attempting an unauthenticated health or API version endpoint call.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk https://<API_SERVER_IP>:6443/api --max-time 5 | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 403 Forbidden response with message 'forbidden: User "system:anonymous"' confirms anonymous auth is enabled but RBAC blocks it. A 401 Unauthorized confirms anonymous auth is disabled. A successful API listing indicates anonymous auth with permissive RBAC.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For kubeadm-managed clusters, check the kubeadm ConfigMap for the apiserver extra arguments that may set anonymous-auth.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap kubeadm-config -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.ClusterConfiguration}' | grep anonymous
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Should show 'anonymous-auth: false' under apiServer extraArgs. Absence means the default (true) applies.

typical_values: true (default, insecure)
false (hardened)

option_description: Indicates whether a host-level firewall, cloud security group, or network ACL enforces that only authorized CIDR ranges can reach the API server port (6443 or 443). False means the control plane port is reachable from workload subnets, the public internet, or any other network without perimeter filtering.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires api_server_unauthenticated_ingress_exposure when api_server_firewall_ingress_restricted is false AND anonymous_auth_enabled is true, and also when both api_server_firewall_ingress_restricted and network_policy_restricts_api_server_egress are false regardless of anonymous auth. Absence of firewall restriction removes the network perimeter layer from the control plane trust boundary, meaning all authentication burden falls solely on application-layer controls which may themselves be misconfigured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On control plane nodes running iptables, list rules filtering inbound traffic to the API server port to verify source IP restrictions.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -E '6443|443'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules should show ACCEPT for specific source CIDRs (admin ranges) and DROP/REJECT for 0.0.0.0/0. No rules or a broad ACCEPT rule indicates unrestricted access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS EKS or EC2-hosted control planes, query the security group rules associated with the control plane nodes or EKS cluster endpoint to verify ingress restrictions.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters 'Name=group-name,Values=*master*,*control-plane*,*apiserver*' --query 'SecurityGroups[*].{ID:GroupId,Rules:IpPermissions}' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ingress rules for port 6443/443 should list specific CIDRs (e.g., corporate VPN range) in IpRanges, not 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GKE, navigate to the GKE cluster's Security section in Google Cloud Console and review 'Control plane authorized networks' to confirm CIDR restrictions are configured.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Google Cloud Console > Kubernetes Engine > Clusters > [cluster name] > Details tab > Security > Control plane authorized networks
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Authorized networks should list one or more specific CIDR ranges. 'Not configured' or '0.0.0.0/0' indicates unrestricted access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a workload pod or an unauthorized IP, attempt a TCP connection to the API server port to verify whether the firewall blocks the connection at the network layer.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl run net-test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sh -c 'nc -zvw3 <API_SERVER_IP> 6443; echo exit:$?'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection should time out or be refused if firewall restrictions are in place. A successful connection ('open') indicates the firewall is not restricting pod-to-API-server traffic.

typical_values: false (default in many self-managed clusters)
true (managed services like GKE/EKS with authorized networks enabled)

option_description: Indicates whether Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources in workload namespaces explicitly deny or restrict pod-initiated egress connections to the API server port (6443/443). When false, all pods can freely initiate connections to the control plane regardless of their workload purpose.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers api_server_unauthenticated_ingress_exposure in two conditions where this is false: (1) when false AND anonymous_auth_enabled is true; and (2) when both this and api_server_firewall_ingress_restricted are false. Without egress NetworkPolicy, every pod in every namespace has a direct network path to the control plane, meaning a compromised workload can immediately attempt API server interactions, token replay attacks, or anonymous probing without crossing any network enforcement layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all NetworkPolicy resources across namespaces and filter for those referencing the API server port or implementing default-deny egress to identify coverage.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -A 20 'egress' | grep -E 'port|6443|443|to:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show NetworkPolicy egress rules with port 6443 or 443 explicitly denied or restricted. No output indicates no egress NetworkPolicy targeting the API server exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for default-deny egress policies in each workload namespace, which would block API server traffic unless explicitly permitted.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | python3 -c "import json,sys; nps=json.load(sys.stdin)['items']; [print(np['metadata']['namespace'], np['metadata']['name']) for np in nps if np['spec'].get('policyTypes') and 'Egress' in np['spec']['policyTypes'] and not np['spec'].get('egress')]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lists namespaces with default-deny egress policies. Empty output means no default-deny egress policies exist and pods have unrestricted egress to the API server.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify workload namespaces that have no NetworkPolicy at all, confirming they have fully open pod egress including to the API server.
how_to_obtain.command: for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do count=$(kubectl get networkpolicy -n $ns --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l); [ "$count" -eq 0 ] && echo "No NetworkPolicy: $ns"; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any namespace listed has no NetworkPolicy enforcement. Namespaces like 'default', 'production', or application namespaces appearing here indicate uncontrolled API server egress paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From within a workload pod, test whether a TCP connection to the API server port succeeds to confirm NetworkPolicy is not blocking egress.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl run egress-test --rm -it --image=busybox -n default --restart=Never -- sh -c 'nc -zvw3 kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local 443; echo result:$?'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A successful connection ('open', exit code 0) confirms NetworkPolicy is NOT restricting pod-to-API-server egress. A timeout or connection refused confirms restriction is in place.

typical_values: false (default; most clusters have no egress NetworkPolicy to control plane)
true (hardened environments with explicit egress deny policies)

option_description: Identifies whether a Kubernetes role binding is cluster-scoped (ClusterRoleBinding, granting permissions across all namespaces) or namespace-scoped (RoleBinding, restricting permissions to a single namespace). This determines the blast radius of the permissions granted by the binding.
security_impact: The Rego policy for overpermissive_rbac_role_binding_propagation fires on BOTH cluster and namespace scope values when combined with bound_role_has_wildcard_or_admin=true, subject_type=ServiceAccount, and service_account_automounts_token=true. Cluster-scoped bindings are inherently higher risk as they grant cross-namespace authority, enabling a compromised pod to interact with any namespace's resources. Namespace-scoped bindings with wildcard permissions still represent a full trust boundary breach within that namespace, which may be sufficient for lateral movement to the control plane.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all ClusterRoleBindings to identify cluster-scoped bindings, which grant permissions across all namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,ROLE:.roleRef.name,SUBJECTS:.subjects[*].kind' --no-headers
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each line represents a cluster-scoped binding. Pay attention to bindings where ROLE shows 'cluster-admin' or custom roles, and SUBJECTS shows 'ServiceAccount'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all namespace-scoped RoleBindings across all namespaces to identify namespace-scoped bindings.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,ROLE:.roleRef.name,SUBJECTS:.subjects[*].kind' --no-headers
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each line represents a namespace-scoped binding. Note the namespace column to understand the scope of permissions granted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Specifically identify the resource kind of a named binding to definitively determine its scope (ClusterRoleBinding vs RoleBinding).
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebinding,rolebinding --all-namespaces -o json | python3 -c "import json,sys; items=json.load(sys.stdin)['items']; [print(i['kind'], i['metadata'].get('namespace','cluster-wide'), i['metadata']['name']) for i in items]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ClusterRoleBinding entries show 'cluster-wide' for namespace. RoleBinding entries show their specific namespace. The 'kind' field definitively identifies scope.

typical_values: cluster (ClusterRoleBinding - higher risk, cross-namespace)
namespace (RoleBinding - limited to single namespace)

option_description: Indicates whether the role referenced by a binding grants wildcard verbs (verbs: ['*']), wildcard resources (resources: ['*']), or is the built-in cluster-admin ClusterRole. Such permissions represent effectively unrestricted API access within the binding's scope.
security_impact: This is a required true condition in both Rego trigger paths for overpermissive_rbac_role_binding_propagation. Combined with ServiceAccount subject type and token auto-mounting, wildcard or admin roles attached to any service account create a direct trust propagation path from the workload zone to the control plane. A pod inheriting cluster-admin effectively becomes a control plane administrator, capable of reading all secrets, modifying RBAC, scheduling privileged pods, or deleting cluster resources without exploiting any vulnerability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify all ClusterRoleBindings referencing the built-in cluster-admin role, which represents the highest privilege level.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | python3 -c "import json,sys; items=json.load(sys.stdin)['items']; [print(i['metadata']['name'], [s.get('name') for s in i.get('subjects',[])]) for i in items if i['roleRef']['name']=='cluster-admin']"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lists all bindings to cluster-admin. Any binding referencing a service account or non-admin user is a critical finding. Only system components should appear here.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect ClusterRole and Role definitions for wildcard verbs or resources that grant effectively unrestricted permissions.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterroles,roles --all-namespaces -o json | python3 -c "import json,sys; items=json.load(sys.stdin)['items']; [print(i['kind'], i['metadata']['name'], r) for i in items for r in i.get('rules',[]) if '*' in r.get('verbs',[]) or '*' in r.get('resources',[])]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lists roles with wildcard rules. System roles like 'cluster-admin' are expected. Custom roles (e.g., 'app-operator') appearing here are high-risk findings requiring review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For a specific role binding, extract the referenced role name and inspect its rules to determine if wildcards or admin permissions are present.
how_to_obtain.command: ROLE=$(kubectl get clusterrolebinding <BINDING_NAME> -o jsonpath='{.roleRef.name}'); kubectl get clusterrole $ROLE -o jsonpath='{.rules}' | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules output showing 'verbs: ["*"]' or 'resources: ["*"]' confirms wildcard permissions. Clean rules with specific verbs (get, list, watch) and specific resources indicate least-privilege design.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use kubectl auth reconcile dry-run or the rakkess/kubectl-who-can plugin to enumerate effective permissions for a specific service account across the cluster.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl-who-can get secrets --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null || kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<NAMESPACE>:<SA_NAME>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A long list of allowed resources, especially 'secrets' get/list across all namespaces, or '*' permissions, confirms wildcard or admin-equivalent role binding.

typical_values: false (expected for application service accounts with least-privilege roles)
true (misconfigured; commonly found in CI/CD service accounts, operators, and legacy deployments)

option_description: Identifies the kind of principal referenced as the subject in a role binding: ServiceAccount (a Kubernetes-managed identity used by pods), User (a human or external identity), or Group (a collection of users or system groups). ServiceAccount subjects are particularly significant because they create automatic credential delivery into running pods.
security_impact: The Rego policy for overpermissive_rbac_role_binding_propagation specifically requires subject_type=ServiceAccount to fire. This is because ServiceAccounts uniquely create an automatic workload-to-control-plane privilege propagation path: the token is auto-mounted into pods, meaning any container compromise immediately grants the bound RBAC permissions. User and Group subjects require explicit credential theft from a human operator, while ServiceAccount compromise is inherent to pod compromise, making it a direct trust zone boundary crossing mechanism.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all ClusterRoleBindings with their subject types to identify ServiceAccount subjects bound to cluster-scoped roles.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | python3 -c "import json,sys; items=json.load(sys.stdin)['items']; [print(i['metadata']['name'], i['roleRef']['name'], s['kind'], s.get('namespace',''), s.get('name','')) for i in items for s in i.get('subjects',[])]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each line shows binding name, role name, subject kind (ServiceAccount/User/Group), namespace, and subject name. ServiceAccount entries with powerful roles are immediate findings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Filter all role bindings across all namespaces to show only those with ServiceAccount subjects, which represent workload-to-control-plane privilege paths.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | python3 -c "import json,sys; items=json.load(sys.stdin)['items']; [print(i['kind'], i['metadata'].get('namespace',''), i['metadata']['name'], s['name']) for i in items for s in i.get('subjects',[]) if s['kind']=='ServiceAccount']"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lists all ServiceAccount-subject bindings. Cross-reference with bound role permissions to identify over-privileged service accounts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For a specific binding, extract and display the subjects array to identify kind, name, and namespace of all principals.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebinding <BINDING_NAME> -o jsonpath='{.subjects}' | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output showing subject entries with 'kind' field. 'ServiceAccount' kind with a 'namespace' field confirms a workload identity. 'User' or 'Group' kind indicates human or external identity.

typical_values: ServiceAccount (most common in automation, operators, CI/CD pipelines)
User (human operators, CI/CD external identities)
Group (system:masters, system:authenticated groups)

option_description: Controls whether the Kubernetes API token for a service account is automatically projected into pods as a volume mount at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. When true (the default), every pod using the service account receives a valid API credential without any explicit configuration, enabling it to authenticate to the API server.
security_impact: This attribute appears in two Rego rules. For overpermissive_rbac_role_binding_propagation, it is a required condition alongside ServiceAccount subject type and wildcard/admin role: without the token being mounted, the RBAC permissions cannot be exercised from within the pod. For service_account_token_cross_zone_exfiltration, the absence of this control (combined with no egress NetworkPolicy) triggers the exposure, because auto-mounted tokens provide the credential that enables cross-zone API authentication from a compromised pod. Disabling auto-mounting eliminates the automatic credential delivery mechanism that turns pod compromise into control plane access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the automountServiceAccountToken field on ServiceAccount objects to identify accounts with auto-mounting explicitly disabled or relying on the insecure default.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get serviceaccounts --all-namespaces -o json | python3 -c "import json,sys; items=json.load(sys.stdin)['items']; [print(i['metadata']['namespace'], i['metadata']['name'], i.get('automountServiceAccountToken', 'NOT_SET(default=true)')) for i in items]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each line shows namespace, SA name, and automount setting. 'NOT_SET' or 'true' means tokens are auto-mounted. Only 'false' explicitly disables auto-mounting.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check individual pod specs for the automountServiceAccountToken override, as pod-level settings override the ServiceAccount-level setting.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | python3 -c "import json,sys; items=json.load(sys.stdin)['items']; [print(i['metadata']['namespace'], i['metadata']['name'], i['spec'].get('automountServiceAccountToken', 'NOT_SET(inherits_SA)')) for i in items]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pod-level 'false' overrides a ServiceAccount-level 'true'. 'NOT_SET' means the pod inherits the ServiceAccount setting. Focus on pods where both SA and pod spec show true or NOT_SET.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify token mount status in a running pod by checking the mounted volume at the default service account token path.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <NAMESPACE> <POD_NAME> -- ls -la /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ 2>/dev/null && echo 'TOKEN MOUNTED' || echo 'NO TOKEN MOUNTED'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'TOKEN MOUNTED' with files (token, ca.crt, namespace) confirms auto-mounting is active. 'NO TOKEN MOUNTED' or a directory not found error confirms token auto-mounting is disabled for this pod.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify the default service account in each namespace, which is used by pods that do not explicitly specify a service account and typically has auto-mounting enabled by default.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get serviceaccount default --all-namespaces -o json | python3 -c "import json,sys; items=json.load(sys.stdin)['items']; [print(i['metadata']['namespace'], i.get('automountServiceAccountToken','NOT_SET(default=true)')) for i in items]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Shows automount setting for the default SA in each namespace. 'NOT_SET' across most namespaces indicates a systemic risk where all pods without explicit SA assignment auto-mount tokens.

typical_values: true (Kubernetes default; most clusters have not disabled this)
false (hardened deployments; explicitly set on SA and/or pod spec)

option_description: Controls whether network-level segmentation (firewall rules, cloud security groups, or Kubernetes NetworkPolicy) enforces that only the API server IP(s) can reach etcd client ports 2379 and 2380. When false, etcd is reachable from nodes, pods, or other cluster-internal actors beyond the API server.
security_impact: The Rego rule etcd_direct_access_bypass_of_api_server_boundary fires when this is false and either etcd_client_cert_auth_enabled is also false or etcd_listen_address_scope is all_interfaces. Direct etcd access bypasses all API server authn/authz and admission controls, allowing any actor with network reach to read or write all cluster state including Secrets. This collapses the control plane trust boundary to the etcd network perimeter alone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a worker node or test pod, attempt a TCP connection to the etcd client port to determine reachability from outside the API server.
how_to_obtain.command: nc -zv <etcd-node-ip> 2379 2>/dev/null && echo 'REACHABLE' || echo 'BLOCKED'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: BLOCKED indicates network controls are in place; REACHABLE indicates etcd is accessible from this network segment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a cloud-hosted cluster, inspect security group rules associated with the control plane nodes to verify inbound rules on ports 2379/2380 are scoped to the API server IP only.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=group-name,Values='*control-plane*' --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions[?FromPort==`2379` || FromPort==`2380`]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules should list only the API server private IP CIDR as the source; any broader CIDR (e.g., 0.0.0.0/0 or cluster VPC range) indicates over-permissive access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources in the kube-system namespace to verify egress toward etcd ports is restricted to the API server.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A 20 'etcd\|2379\|2380'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A NetworkPolicy selecting etcd pods should show an ingress rule permitting only the API server pod or IP on ports 2379 and 2380.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Deploy a debug pod in a non-system namespace and attempt a curl or openssl connection to etcd to confirm cross-namespace network isolation.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl run etcd-reachability-test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sh -c 'nc -zv <etcd-ip> 2379; echo exit_code=$?'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-zero exit code or connection refused/timeout confirms etcd is not reachable from workload namespaces.

typical_values: true (hardened clusters with firewall/SG rules or NetworkPolicy)
false (default kubeadm clusters without additional network controls)

option_description: Controls whether etcd enforces mutual TLS client certificate authentication for all incoming client connections via the --client-cert-auth=true startup flag. When disabled, any client that can reach the etcd port can interact with the datastore without presenting a valid certificate.
security_impact: The Rego rule etcd_direct_access_bypass_of_api_server_boundary fires when this is false alongside etcd_network_access_restricted_to_api_server being false, or when etcd_listen_address_scope is all_interfaces with this also false. Without client certificate authentication, an attacker who reaches etcd over the network can read all cluster state including Secrets, ConfigMaps, and RBAC policies, and can write arbitrary state to manipulate scheduling or inject malicious workloads — all without any API server-enforced policy layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the etcd static pod manifest on the control plane node to check the --client-cert-auth flag value.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml | grep -E 'client-cert-auth|listen-client'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Should contain '--client-cert-auth=true'; absence of this flag or 'false' value indicates authentication is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the running etcd process arguments directly from the node to confirm the live configuration matches the manifest.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep etcd | grep -o -- '--client-cert-auth[^ ]*'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: '--client-cert-auth=true' should appear in the process arguments; missing flag means the default (which varies by version) or false is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the etcd pod specification via the Kubernetes API to retrieve the actual container command arguments.
how_to_obtain.command:
kubectl get pod -n kube-system -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].command}' | tr ',' '
' | grep client-cert-auth
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should be '--client-cert-auth=true'; empty output or false value indicates the flag is absent or disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt an unauthenticated connection to the etcd endpoint to verify whether client certificate is required.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -k https://<etcd-ip>:2379/v3/auth/status --max-time 5 2>&1 | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A TLS handshake error requiring client certificate (e.g., 'tls: certificate required') confirms auth is enforced; a successful JSON response without a certificate indicates auth is disabled.

typical_values: true (kubeadm-provisioned clusters, managed Kubernetes services)
false (manually configured or legacy clusters without hardening)

option_description: Describes the network interface binding scope for etcd client port connections as determined by the --listen-client-urls configuration. loopback_only restricts to 127.0.0.1 (same host only); node_local binds to the node's primary network interface IP; all_interfaces binds to 0.0.0.0, making etcd reachable from any network interface including cluster and pod networks.
security_impact: Two Rego rule conditions in etcd_direct_access_bypass_of_api_server_boundary reference this attribute: when all_interfaces is set without network access restriction, and when all_interfaces is set without client cert auth. Binding to 0.0.0.0 maximally expands the etcd attack surface by making it reachable from pod networks, node networks, and potentially external networks, meaning any compromise of network segmentation directly exposes the authoritative cluster state store.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read the etcd static pod manifest and extract the --listen-client-urls value to determine the binding address.
how_to_obtain.command: grep 'listen-client-urls' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'https://127.0.0.1:2379' indicates loopback_only; a specific node IP (e.g., https://10.0.0.5:2379) indicates node_local; 'https://0.0.0.0:2379' indicates all_interfaces.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the live etcd process arguments for the listen-client-urls parameter to confirm the runtime binding.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep '[e]tcd' | grep -o -- '--listen-client-urls=[^ ]*'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The URL scheme and address indicate scope: 127.0.0.1 = loopback_only, a routable IP = node_local, 0.0.0.0 = all_interfaces.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use ss or netstat on the control plane node to verify which addresses the etcd process is actually listening on at runtime.
how_to_obtain.command: ss -tlnp | grep 2379
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Local address column showing '127.0.0.1:2379' = loopback_only; specific node IP = node_local; '0.0.0.0:2379' or '*:2379' = all_interfaces.

typical_values: loopback_only (kubeadm single-node or stacked etcd topology)
node_local (stacked etcd with node IP binding, common in kubeadm HA)
all_interfaces (misconfigured or legacy deployments)

option_description: Represents the union of all HTTP operation types (CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE, CONNECT) explicitly listed in rules[].operations fields across all registered MutatingWebhookConfiguration and ValidatingWebhookConfiguration objects. Operations absent from this list are not intercepted by any webhook, creating policy enforcement blind spots.
security_impact: The Rego rule admission_webhook_bypass_via_scope_gap fires when UPDATE is not present in this array. UPDATE operations on existing pods or workloads are a primary vector for privilege escalation and policy bypass — an attacker can CREATE a compliant workload, then UPDATE it to add privileged containers or security context overrides after the creation-time webhook check. Gaps in DELETE or CONNECT coverage may allow unauthorized resource removal or API tunneling without policy inspection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all distinct operations values from every registered webhook configuration and aggregate them into a deduplicated list.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '[.items[].webhooks[].rules[].operations[]] | unique | .[]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Should list CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE, and optionally CONNECT; absence of UPDATE is a critical gap indicating policy bypass is possible on modifications.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List each webhook by name alongside its covered operations to identify which specific webhooks lack UPDATE or other operations coverage.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $name | .webhooks[] | [$name, .name, (.rules[].operations | join(","))] | join(" | ")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table of webhook names and their operations; rows showing only CREATE without UPDATE identify the source of coverage gaps.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Kubernetes REST API to retrieve webhook configurations and parse operations fields programmatically for automated assessment.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -k -H 'Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)' https://kubernetes.default.svc/apis/admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1/mutatingwebhookconfigurations | python3 -c "import sys,json; data=json.load(sys.stdin); ops=set(); [ops.update(r.get('operations',[])) for item in data['items'] for wh in item.get('webhooks',[]) for r in wh.get('rules',[])]; print(sorted(ops))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A Python list such as ['CREATE', 'UPDATE'] — missing operations compared to ['CONNECT', 'CREATE', 'DELETE', 'UPDATE'] indicate gaps.

typical_values: ['CREATE'] (minimal webhook configurations covering only resource creation)
['CREATE', 'UPDATE'] (moderate coverage, missing DELETE and CONNECT)
['CREATE', 'UPDATE', 'DELETE', 'CONNECT'] (comprehensive coverage, security-hardened deployments)

option_description: Represents the list of Kubernetes subresources explicitly included in admission webhook rules across all registered webhook configurations, identified by slash-containing entries in rules[].resources[] (e.g., pods/exec, pods/ephemeralcontainers, pods/attach). Subresources absent from this list are not subject to webhook policy inspection.
security_impact: The Rego rule admission_webhook_bypass_via_scope_gap fires independently when pods/exec is missing from this array and when pods/ephemeralcontainers is missing. These subresources are high-value attack vectors: pods/exec allows arbitrary command execution in running containers without creating a new workload, bypassing admission checks on pods; pods/ephemeralcontainers enables injection of debugging containers with elevated capabilities into existing pods. An attacker who can CREATE a compliant pod can later exec into it or inject an ephemeral container to achieve privilege escalation, entirely bypassing webhook enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all subresource entries (those containing a slash) from webhook rules across all webhook configurations.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '[.items[].webhooks[].rules[].resources[] | select(contains("/"))] | unique | .[]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Should include pods/exec, pods/ephemeralcontainers, and pods/attach at minimum; empty output or missing high-risk subresources indicates enforcement gaps.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check specifically whether pods/exec and pods/ephemeralcontainers are covered by any webhook, as these are the Rego-referenced critical subresources.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '[.items[].webhooks[].rules[].resources[]] | unique' | grep -E 'pods/exec|pods/ephemeralcontainers|pods/attach'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines matching 'pods/exec' and 'pods/ephemeralcontainers' confirm coverage; absence of either is a critical gap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List each webhook name alongside its resource entries to identify which webhooks, if any, cover subresources and which cover only top-level resources.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $n | .webhooks[] | .name as $w | .rules[] | .resources[] | select(contains("/")) | [$n, $w, .] | join(" > ")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each line shows a webhook covering a specific subresource; no output indicates zero subresource coverage across all validating webhooks.

typical_values: [] (most default deployments — subresources are not covered by OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno unless explicitly configured)
['pods/exec', 'pods/attach'] (partial coverage by security-focused webhook policies)
['pods/exec', 'pods/ephemeralcontainers', 'pods/attach', 'pods/portforward'] (hardened policy suites)

option_description: Indicates whether any registered admission webhook defines a namespaceSelector field that restricts which namespaces the webhook applies to, potentially excluding one or more non-system tenant namespaces from policy inspection. Used dually: to detect bypass gaps (any webhook excluding tenant namespaces) and to assess multi-tenant enforcement (all webhooks having scoped selectors).
security_impact: The Rego rule admission_webhook_bypass_via_scope_gap fires when this is true, because a namespaceSelector that excludes namespaces means at least some tenant namespaces bypass webhook inspection entirely — requests in excluded namespaces traverse the control plane boundary without policy enforcement. Conversely, the Rego rule namespace_boundary_non_enforcement_in_multi_tenant_control_plane fires when this is false, because absent namespace selectors means webhooks either apply to all namespaces (including system namespaces, risking interference) or are not scoped for per-tenant enforcement. Both conditions represent enforcement configuration risks at the admission boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve all webhook configurations and display their namespaceSelector fields to determine scope restrictions.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o yaml | grep -A 10 'namespaceSelector'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of namespaceSelector with matchLabels or matchExpressions that exclude tenant namespaces (e.g., not matching 'env: production') indicates a bypass gap; complete absence may indicate either global coverage or missing multi-tenant scoping.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate which specific namespaces are excluded by any webhook namespaceSelector by checking namespace labels against selector criteria.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $n | .webhooks[] | select(.namespaceSelector != null) | [$n, .name, (.namespaceSelector | tostring)] | join(" | ")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON representation of each namespaceSelector showing matchLabels/matchExpressions; compare against actual namespace labels to identify excluded namespaces.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all namespaces and their labels, then manually cross-reference against webhook namespaceSelectors to identify which namespaces fall outside webhook coverage.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get namespaces --show-labels | grep -v 'control-plane\|kube-system\|kube-public'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Namespaces whose labels do not match any webhook's namespaceSelector matchLabels are excluded from webhook enforcement — these represent policy bypass surfaces.

typical_values: false (most default deployments where webhooks apply cluster-wide without namespace filtering)
true (clusters using OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno with namespace exemptions for system or monitoring namespaces)

option_description: Indicates whether the aggregate admission webhook rule set includes coverage for high-risk Kubernetes API groups: the core group ('') for pods and secrets, apps for deployments and daemonsets, and batch for jobs and cronjobs. False means one or more of these API groups lack webhook coverage, leaving privileged workload creation paths uninspected by policy enforcement.
security_impact: The Rego rule admission_webhook_bypass_via_scope_gap fires when this is false. The core API group ('') covers Pods and Secrets — the most direct surfaces for workload privilege escalation and secret exfiltration. The apps group covers Deployments and DaemonSets, which can persistently schedule privileged containers across the cluster. The batch group covers Jobs and CronJobs, which can execute privileged or exfiltrating workloads on a schedule. Missing coverage in any of these groups means an attacker can create or modify workloads of those types without any admission policy inspection, directly bypassing the control plane policy enforcement boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all distinct apiGroups values across all webhook rules and verify that the core group (''), 'apps', and 'batch' are all present.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '[.items[].webhooks[].rules[].apiGroups[]] | unique | .[]' | sort
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should include an empty string (core group ''), 'apps', and 'batch'; missing entries indicate uncovered API groups.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check specifically for core group coverage (represented as empty string or '*') across all webhook rules.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '[.items[].webhooks[].rules[].apiGroups[]] | map(select(. == "" or . == "*")) | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count greater than 0 confirms core group coverage; 0 means pods, secrets, services, and other core resources are uninspected by any webhook.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For each high-risk API group, verify which specific resource types are covered by webhook rules to confirm meaningful coverage beyond just the group name.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[].webhooks[].rules[] | select(.apiGroups[] | . == "" or . == "apps" or . == "batch") | [.apiGroups[], (.resources | join(","))] | join(" -> ")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines mapping API groups to their covered resources; should include '' -> pods,secrets and apps -> deployments,daemonsets and batch -> jobs,cronjobs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Kubernetes API to programmatically validate that the three critical API groups are all covered and output a compliance summary.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); grps=set(); [grps.update(r.get('apiGroups',[])) for i in d['items'] for w in i.get('webhooks',[]) for r in w.get('rules',[])]; required={'','apps','batch'}; print('COVERED:', required.issubset(grps), '| Missing:', required-grps)"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'COVERED: True | Missing: set()' confirms full coverage; any missing groups are listed explicitly.

typical_values: false (minimal webhook deployments covering only specific custom resources or a single namespace)
true (OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno installations with comprehensive base constraint library covering standard Kubernetes resource types)

option_description: Describes the failurePolicy setting for registered admission webhooks, which governs behavior when a webhook server is unreachable, times out, or returns an error. 'Fail' causes the API request to be rejected when the webhook cannot be consulted. 'Ignore' causes the API server to allow the request through as if the webhook approved it, regardless of the error condition.
security_impact: The Rego rule admission_webhook_bypass_via_scope_gap references this attribute in the context of scope gaps — Ignore compounds coverage gaps because even attempted webhook calls that error out result in unconditional approval. The Rego rule admission_webhook_server_trust_inversion fires when webhook_server_zone is workload_zone and this is Ignore: a workload-zone webhook server that is compromised, overloaded, or deliberately taken down will cause all requests to be approved without enforcement, allowing an attacker to bypass policy by simply making the webhook unavailable. This means Ignore effectively creates an availability-dependent security control, which is an architectural weakness at the admission enforcement boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract the failurePolicy value for every webhook across all MutatingWebhookConfiguration and ValidatingWebhookConfiguration objects.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $cfg | .webhooks[] | [$cfg, .name, .failurePolicy] | join(" | ")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table of config name, webhook name, and policy value; any row showing 'Ignore' for a security-critical webhook indicates a risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Count the number of webhooks using Ignore vs Fail to understand the overall posture and identify which webhook configurations contain Ignore-policy webhooks.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '{Fail: [.items[].webhooks[] | select(.failurePolicy=="Fail")] | length, Ignore: [.items[].webhooks[] | select(.failurePolicy=="Ignore")] | length}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON with counts for each policy; any Ignore count greater than 0 for security-enforcing (not just observability) webhooks warrants review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List only webhooks explicitly configured with Ignore policy to produce a targeted remediation list.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $n | .webhooks[] | select(.failurePolicy=="Ignore") | [$n, .name] | @csv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CSV rows identifying each webhook configuration and webhook name using Ignore; empty output confirms all webhooks use Fail policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review webhook deployment procedures with platform operators to determine whether Ignore is intentionally set for availability reasons and whether compensating controls (webhook HA, PodDisruptionBudget, separate webhook namespace) are in place.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Interview the platform team and review Helm chart values or Kustomize overlays used to deploy OPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno, or custom webhooks — look for failurePolicy overrides in values.yaml or webhook manifest patches.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation confirming Fail is set for all security-enforcing webhooks, or explicit risk acceptance with compensating controls documented for any Ignore policy webhooks.

typical_values: Ignore (default for many webhook operator installations to prevent availability impact during initial deployment)
Fail (hardened configurations and production security-critical webhook policies)
Mixed (common in real clusters — observability or mutation webhooks use Ignore, validation webhooks use Fail)

option_description: Identifies the network zone where the admission webhook server is deployed — either control_plane_zone (dedicated, hardened), shared_zone (shared infrastructure), or workload_zone (operator-controlled tenant space). This zone classification determines the trust boundary relationship between the API server and its policy enforcement delegates.
security_impact: The Rego rule admission_webhook_server_trust_inversion fires when webhook_server_zone equals workload_zone and either the CA bundle is absent or the failure policy is Ignore. A webhook in the workload zone is controlled by workload operators who may be compromised, allowing them to return fraudulent admission decisions. When combined with unrestricted RBAC on the webhook operator, even a shared_zone placement triggers the finding, because the webhook operator can directly manipulate cluster state as well as subvert policy enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all ValidatingWebhookConfigurations and MutatingWebhookConfigurations, then extract the clientConfig service namespace or URL to determine the deployment zone of each webhook server.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $name | .webhooks[]? | [$name, .name, (.clientConfig.service.namespace // .clientConfig.url // "no-service")] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Tab-separated rows showing webhook config name, webhook name, and the service namespace or URL. Namespaces like kube-system or cert-manager suggest control_plane_zone or shared_zone; tenant or application namespaces indicate workload_zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Cross-reference the identified webhook server namespace against your network zone topology by checking which node pool or subnet the webhook server pod runs on.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod -n <webhook-namespace> -o wide -l <webhook-selector> --show-labels
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pod listing showing node name and IP. Match the node or IP range against your documented zone CIDR map to classify as control_plane_zone, shared_zone, or workload_zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API directly to retrieve webhook configurations in JSON for programmatic zone classification.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl create token default)" https://<apiserver>:6443/apis/admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1/validatingwebhookconfigurations | jq '.items[].webhooks[].clientConfig'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects containing either a service block with namespace and name, or a url field. Map namespace values to zones using your topology documentation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview platform or cluster administrators to confirm the intended zone classification of each webhook server and verify it matches network zone topology documentation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written confirmation mapping each webhook server service or URL to its network zone classification, consistent with the kubectl output.

typical_values: workload_zone (common in operator-deployed policy engines like OPA/Gatekeeper in tenant namespaces)
shared_zone (common for shared admission controllers in dedicated add-on namespaces)
control_plane_zone (least common, seen in managed Kubernetes offerings)

option_description: Indicates whether a Base64-encoded CA certificate bundle is explicitly set in the caBundle field of each webhook's clientConfig, enabling the API server to perform TLS verification of the webhook server's certificate. When absent, the API server either uses the cluster CA or skips verification entirely, making the webhook endpoint susceptible to interception.
security_impact: The Rego rule admission_webhook_server_trust_inversion triggers when webhook_server_zone is workload_zone and webhook_ca_bundle_configured is false, or when the zone is workload_zone or shared_zone and both the CA bundle is absent and webhook_operator_rbac_unrestricted is true. Without a configured CA bundle, the API server cannot cryptographically verify it is communicating with the legitimate webhook server, allowing a man-in-the-middle or a rogue service at the same DNS name to return arbitrary admission decisions, completely subverting policy enforcement at the control plane boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract the caBundle value from all webhook configurations. A non-empty, non-null value indicates the bundle is configured.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '.items[] | .metadata.name as $cfg | .webhooks[]? | {config: $cfg, webhook: .name, caBundle_set: (.clientConfig.caBundle != null and .clientConfig.caBundle != "")}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects with caBundle_set: true for each webhook indicate the field is populated. Any false value means the CA bundle is not configured for that webhook.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Decode and inspect the actual CA certificate content to verify it is valid and matches the webhook server's TLS certificate issuer.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> -o jsonpath='{.webhooks[0].clientConfig.caBundle}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Certificate subject, issuer, and validity dates. Compare issuer against the webhook server's TLS certificate to confirm the bundle pins the correct CA.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve webhook configuration via the Kubernetes REST API and filter for the caBundle field presence.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '[.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, webhooks: [.webhooks[]? | {name: .name, has_ca_bundle: (.clientConfig.caBundle | length > 0)}]}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array showing each webhook configuration and per-webhook boolean for CA bundle presence. All entries should show has_ca_bundle: true for a passing state.

typical_values: false (common in development clusters or self-managed operators that rely on cert-manager injection but have not yet rotated the bundle)
true (expected in production; cert-manager and similar tools inject caBundle via MutatingWebhookConfiguration annotation)

option_description: Indicates whether the service account bound to the webhook server pod holds cluster-admin or equivalent permissions (wildcard verbs on all resources cluster-wide). When true, a compromised webhook server process has both the ability to return fraudulent admission decisions and to directly issue privileged API server requests, compounding the trust inversion risk.
security_impact: The Rego rule admission_webhook_server_trust_inversion includes a condition where webhook_server_zone is workload_zone or shared_zone, webhook_ca_bundle_configured is false, and webhook_operator_rbac_unrestricted is true. This combination represents the highest-severity trust inversion scenario: the webhook operator is not cryptographically verified, resides in a less-trusted zone, and its service account can directly alter cluster state. An attacker compromising this webhook gains both policy bypass and direct control plane write access in a single step.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify the service account used by the webhook server pod, then test its effective permissions cluster-wide.
how_to_obtain.command: SA=$(kubectl get pod -n <webhook-namespace> <webhook-pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}'); kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --as=system:serviceaccount:<webhook-namespace>:$SA --all-namespaces
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'yes' confirms unrestricted cluster-admin equivalent access (true). Output of 'no' indicates restricted permissions (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all ClusterRoleBindings and RoleBindings that reference the webhook server's service account to identify which roles are granted.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o json | jq --arg sa '<sa-name>' --arg ns '<webhook-namespace>' '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | select(.kind=="ServiceAccount" and .name==$sa and .namespace==$ns)) | {kind: .kind, name: .metadata.name, role: .roleRef.name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of role bindings. Presence of cluster-admin, admin, or roles with wildcard verbs (verbs: ["*"]) on wildcard resources indicates webhook_operator_rbac_unrestricted should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the specific ClusterRole or Role definition to confirm wildcard verb or resource coverage.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrole <role-name> -o json | jq '.rules[] | select(.verbs[] == "*" or .resources[] == "*")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-empty output confirms wildcard permissions exist in the role, indicating unrestricted access. Empty output suggests the role is appropriately scoped.

typical_values: true (common with OPA/Gatekeeper default installations that request cluster-admin for ease of deployment)
false (hardened deployments where webhook operators are granted only the specific get/list/watch permissions they require)

option_description: Indicates whether Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects exist in workload namespaces with explicit egress deny or allow rules that restrict outbound TCP traffic on ports 443 and 6443 toward control plane IP ranges. This control limits the ability of compromised pods to directly contact the API server using mounted service account tokens.
security_impact: The Rego rule service_account_token_cross_zone_exfiltration fires when service_account_automounts_token is not disabled and egress_network_policy_controls_control_plane_ports is false. Without egress restriction, a compromised pod can use its auto-mounted token to make authenticated API server requests or exfiltrate the token for use from external locations. The absence of this control removes the network enforcement layer that would otherwise contain a token-bearing compromised workload within the workload zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all NetworkPolicy objects across all namespaces and filter for egress rules targeting control plane ports 443 and 6443.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.egress != null) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, egress_ports: [.spec.egress[].ports[]? | select(.port == 443 or .port == 6443)]}' | jq 'select(.egress_ports | length > 0)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects listing namespaces with NetworkPolicies containing egress rules for ports 443 or 6443. Empty output across workload namespaces indicates no such controls exist (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for default-deny egress policies in workload namespaces, which would implicitly block traffic to control plane ports.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector == {} or .spec.podSelector == null) | select(.spec.egress == [] or .spec.egress == null) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, policy_types: .spec.policyTypes}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies with policyTypes containing Egress and empty egress rules represent default-deny egress policies. These should appear in workload namespaces.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a test pod in a workload namespace, attempt a TCP connection to the API server on port 6443 to verify whether egress network policy enforcement is active.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl run nettest --image=busybox --restart=Never -n <workload-namespace> -- sh -c 'nc -zv <api-server-ip> 6443; echo exit:$?'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the connection is refused or times out, egress policy is enforced (true). If it succeeds, no effective egress restriction is in place (false). Clean up with: kubectl delete pod nettest -n <workload-namespace>

typical_values: false (default in most clusters; NetworkPolicy for control plane egress is rarely implemented)
true (found in PCI-DSS or high-security environments with explicit egress allow-listing)

option_description: Indicates whether pods use projected service account tokens with explicit audience and expiration claims (via ServiceAccountToken projected volumes) rather than long-lived legacy tokens stored as Secrets. Bound tokens include an aud claim that restricts valid usage to the intended API server audience and expire automatically, limiting their utility if exfiltrated to external locations.
security_impact: The Rego rule service_account_token_cross_zone_exfiltration includes a condition where service_account_automounts_token is not disabled, egress_network_policy_controls_control_plane_ports is false, and token_bound_to_audience is also false. When all three controls are absent, exfiltrated tokens are long-lived and usable from any location against any API server accepting that audience, representing maximum cross-zone token reuse risk. Audience-bound tokens mitigate this by making tokens invalid outside their intended context.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect pod volume definitions across all namespaces for projected service account token volumes with explicit audience and expiration settings.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes != null) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, pod: .metadata.name, projected_tokens: [.spec.volumes[]? | select(.projected != null) | .projected.sources[]? | select(.serviceAccountToken != null) | .serviceAccountToken]}' | jq 'select(.projected_tokens | length > 0)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Objects showing projected token sources with audience and expirationSeconds fields. Pods lacking this structure and using legacy secret-based tokens indicate token_bound_to_audience is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the API server is configured with the required flags for bound service account tokens.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod kube-apiserver-$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -n kube-system -o json | jq '.spec.containers[0].command[] | select(startswith("--service-account-issuer") or startswith("--api-audiences") or startswith("--service-account-signing-key-file"))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing --service-account-issuer and --api-audiences flags confirm the API server supports bound tokens. Absence of these flags means legacy tokens are in use (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For kubeadm-provisioned clusters, inspect the API server static pod manifest for bound service account token configuration flags.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'service-account-issuer|api-audiences|service-account-signing-key' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Matching lines confirm projected token support is configured. No matches indicate the cluster may be using legacy token infrastructure.

typical_values: true (default in Kubernetes 1.21+ clusters; projected tokens are the default token delivery mechanism)
false (older clusters or those with legacy admission configurations that still mount secret-based tokens)

option_description: Indicates whether Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources with explicit egress stanzas exist in the namespace(s) hosting control plane components (typically kube-system), restricting outbound connections from API server, controller-manager, and scheduler pods. Without this, control plane components can initiate unrestricted outbound connections to any endpoint in the cluster network.
security_impact: The Rego rule network_policy_enforcement_gap_at_control_plane_egress fires in multiple conditions involving this attribute: when control_plane_namespace_egress_networkpolicy_configured is false and the CNI enforces policy, when neither policy nor CNI enforcement exists, and when control plane components run as static pods and no egress policy is configured. Unrestricted egress from control plane components enables exploitation of SSRF or callback vulnerabilities in API server or controller-manager code to reach workload-zone endpoints, blurring the directional trust boundary in ways that workload-level controls cannot compensate for.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all NetworkPolicy objects in kube-system and check for the presence of egress stanzas.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n kube-system -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, has_egress_rules: (.spec.egress != null and (.spec.egress | length) > 0), policy_types: .spec.policyTypes}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects for each policy. Policies with has_egress_rules: true and policyTypes containing Egress indicate egress control is configured (true). Empty items array or all false values indicates no egress NetworkPolicy exists (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check all namespaces that may host control plane components across managed or non-standard deployments.
how_to_obtain.command: for ns in kube-system kube-public; do echo "=== $ns ==="; kubectl get networkpolicy -n $ns -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,POLICY-TYPES:.spec.policyTypes' 2>/dev/null || echo 'none'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each namespace section lists its NetworkPolicies and their policy types. Absence of Egress in policyTypes or no policies at all indicates false for this attribute.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify whether any default-deny egress policy exists in kube-system to ensure completeness of coverage.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n kube-system -o json | jq '.items[] | select((.spec.podSelector == {}) or (.spec.podSelector.matchLabels == null)) | select(.spec.policyTypes[]? == "Egress")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A matching policy indicates a default-deny or broad egress policy exists for control plane pods (true). No output means no such baseline restriction is applied.

typical_values: false (near-universal default; kube-system NetworkPolicy for egress is almost never configured even in enterprise clusters)
true (rare; seen only in highly regulated environments with explicit control plane hardening runbooks)

option_description: Indicates whether the installed Container Network Interface plugin is both capable of enforcing Kubernetes NetworkPolicy and actively enforcing it for pods running in the control plane namespace. CNI plugins such as Calico, Cilium, Antrea, and Weave Net support NetworkPolicy enforcement, while flannel and others do not. Even capable plugins may have enforcement disabled or misconfigured.
security_impact: The Rego rule network_policy_enforcement_gap_at_control_plane_egress fires when cni_plugin_enforces_networkpolicy_in_control_plane_namespace is false regardless of whether NetworkPolicy objects exist, because without CNI enforcement, defined policies have no effect. It also fires when both this attribute and control_plane_namespace_egress_networkpolicy_configured are false, representing a complete absence of egress control. Deploying NetworkPolicy objects without a capable CNI creates a false sense of security where administrators believe egress is restricted but no enforcement actually occurs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the CNI configuration directory on a node to identify the CNI plugin in use.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/cni/net.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null || cat /etc/cni/net.d/*.conflist 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | grep -i 'type\|name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Plugin type field showing calico, cilium, antrea, weave, or flannel. Calico, Cilium, and Antrea confirm NetworkPolicy enforcement capability. Flannel alone indicates no NetworkPolicy support.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify the CNI plugin from the cluster's DaemonSet or deployment resources in kube-system.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get daemonsets,deployments -n kube-system -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.name | test("calico|cilium|antrea|weave|flannel|canal"; "i")) | {name: .metadata.name, kind: .kind}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Resource names matching known CNI plugins. Calico (calico-node), Cilium (cilium), or Antrea (antrea-agent) confirm capable plugins. Flannel alone (kube-flannel-ds) indicates enforcement is unavailable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Calico, verify NetworkPolicy enforcement is not disabled by checking the Calico configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get felixconfiguration default -o json 2>/dev/null | jq '{policy_enforcement: .spec.policySyncPathPrefix, dataplane: .spec.dataplaneDriver}' || kubectl get configmap calico-config -n kube-system -o json | jq '.data'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Calico configuration showing enforcement is active. For Cilium, run: kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium status | grep -i policy

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm with the platform team whether the CNI plugin is configured to enforce NetworkPolicy for static pods or host-network pods in the control plane namespace, as some CNIs exempt these.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written documentation confirming the CNI enforcement scope includes or explicitly excludes control plane namespace pods, and the rationale for any exemptions.

typical_values: false (clusters using flannel as the sole CNI, or cloud-managed clusters where the CNI does not enforce policy in kube-system)
true (clusters using Calico, Cilium, or Antrea with default enforcement enabled)

option_description: Indicates whether Kubernetes control plane components (API server, controller-manager, scheduler, etcd) are deployed as static pods defined by manifest files in the kubelet's staticPodPath directory. Static pods are started directly by the kubelet and may use the host network namespace or otherwise bypass CNI plugin NetworkPolicy enforcement, making any configured NetworkPolicy for the control plane namespace ineffective.
security_impact: The Rego rule network_policy_enforcement_gap_at_control_plane_egress includes a specific condition where control_plane_components_run_as_static_pods_outside_cni is true and control_plane_namespace_egress_networkpolicy_configured is false. This condition reflects that even when a capable CNI is installed and NetworkPolicy objects are defined, static pods with hostNetwork: true operate in the host network namespace rather than a CNI-managed pod network namespace, so CNI eBPF or iptables rules applied to pod interfaces do not intercept their traffic. This renders the control plane egress enforcement gap non-remediable through standard NetworkPolicy mechanisms.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the kubelet's staticPodPath directory for control plane component manifests on a control plane node.
how_to_obtain.command: ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ 2>/dev/null && cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep -E 'hostNetwork|name:' | head -10
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Manifest files named kube-apiserver.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml, and etcd.yaml indicate static pod deployment. The hostNetwork: true field confirms host network namespace usage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify control plane pods and check whether they are annotated as static pods by the kubelet.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.name | test("kube-apiserver|kube-controller|kube-scheduler|etcd")) | {name: .metadata.name, owner_refs: .metadata.ownerReferences, host_network: .spec.hostNetwork, node_name: .spec.nodeName}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pods with no ownerReferences or ownerReferences of kind Node and hostNetwork: true are static pods running outside normal CNI scope. This confirms control_plane_components_run_as_static_pods_outside_cni is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the kubelet configuration to confirm the staticPodPath setting points to a directory containing control plane manifests.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl cat kubelet | grep -i static-pod-path || cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep -i staticPodPath
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A staticPodPath value pointing to /etc/kubernetes/manifests or equivalent confirms static pod deployment of control plane components (true). Absence of this setting or an empty directory indicates managed pod deployment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm with platform engineers whether the CNI plugin vendor documentation explicitly states NetworkPolicy enforcement behavior for static pods and host-network pods, to determine effective enforcement scope.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Vendor documentation or engineer confirmation stating whether the specific CNI plugin enforces NetworkPolicy for host-network or static pods, clarifying whether the enforcement gap applies.

typical_values: true (standard in kubeadm-provisioned clusters, on-premise deployments, and most self-managed Kubernetes installations)
false (managed Kubernetes services like GKE, EKS, AKS where control plane runs outside the customer cluster node network)

option_description: Tracks the highest privilege level granted by credentials embedded in kubeconfig files — ranging from cluster-admin (full control over all cluster resources) through elevated broad RBAC roles, namespace-scoped permissions, to read-only access. This classification determines whether a leaked kubeconfig grants an attacker control-plane-level authority.
security_impact: The Rego rule kubeconfig_credential_isolation_failure fires when kubeconfig_privilege_level is 'cluster_admin' or 'elevated' AND workload_accessible_storage is true. A cluster_admin kubeconfig accessible from the workload zone bypasses all RBAC boundaries entirely — an attacker obtaining it gains unrestricted API server access without exploiting any vulnerability. Even 'elevated' credentials combined with workload-accessible storage and absent credential rotation trigger the exposure, enabling cross-zone trust boundary violation through credential reuse.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract the user and cluster from the kubeconfig, then look up the ClusterRoleBinding or RoleBinding bound to that credential to identify the highest granted role.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.users[*].name}' && kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name == "<username>") | {name: .metadata.name, role: .roleRef.name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ClusterRoleBinding entries mapping the credential to roles; presence of 'cluster-admin' indicates cluster_admin level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the kubeconfig file directly to identify whether it embeds a service account token or certificate, then cross-reference bound roles.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl config view --raw -o json | jq '.users[].user | keys' && kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces --as=<extracted-username>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'yes' response to wildcard can-i confirms cluster-admin or elevated; 'no' indicates namespace_scoped or read_only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Open the kubeconfig file and identify the credential type (token, client-certificate). For service account tokens, decode the JWT payload to extract the bound service account, then check its role bindings.
how_to_obtain.command: cat ~/.kube/config | grep 'token:' | awk '{print $2}' | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "import sys,json; parts=sys.stdin.read().split('.'); import base64; print(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(parts[1]+'==')))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JWT payload shows 'kubernetes.io/serviceaccount' claims; cross-reference service account name against role bindings to determine privilege level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the API server's SelfSubjectAccessReview to programmatically evaluate what the credential can do against critical resources.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl auth can-i --list --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(\*|secrets|pods|nodes)' | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Wildcard verbs on '*' resources at cluster scope confirms cluster_admin; broad verb lists confirm elevated; limited namespace-specific entries indicate namespace_scoped.

typical_values: cluster_admin
elevated
namespace_scoped

option_description: Indicates whether the kubeconfig credentials rely on automatically rotated short-lived tokens — such as OIDC tokens with sub-one-hour TTL, exec-plugin-generated tokens (e.g., aws eks get-token), or Kubernetes projected service account tokens — rather than static long-lived bearer tokens or service account secrets that persist indefinitely until explicitly revoked.
security_impact: The Rego rule kubeconfig_credential_isolation_failure fires when kubeconfig_privilege_level is 'cluster_admin' or 'elevated', workload_accessible_storage is true, AND short_lived_credential_rotation_enabled is false. Long-lived static credentials represent a persistent attack surface: once leaked to the workload zone, they remain valid indefinitely and can be used from any network location to authenticate against the API server, crossing the workload-to-control-plane trust boundary without detection. Short-lived credentials limit the exploitation window to the token's TTL.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the kubeconfig file for the auth-provider or exec section, which indicates short-lived credential plugins are in use.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl config view --raw -o json | jq '.users[].user | {has_exec: (has("exec")), has_auth_provider: (has("auth-provider")), has_token: (has("token")), has_client_cert: (has("client-certificate-data"))}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: has_exec: true or has_auth_provider: true indicates short-lived token plugin; has_token: true with no exec indicates static token (set false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For OIDC credentials, decode the token from the kubeconfig and check the expiry claim to verify TTL is under one hour.
how_to_obtain.command: TOKEN=$(kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.users[0].user.token}'); echo $TOKEN | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E '(exp|iat|iss)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: exp minus iat less than 3600 seconds confirms short-lived OIDC token; absence of exp or large delta indicates static or long-lived credential.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for projected service account tokens by examining the volume mounts in pods or the exec plugin command in kubeconfig for managed cluster CLIs.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.users[*].user.exec.command}' && kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.users[*].user.exec.args}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Commands like 'aws', 'gke-gcloud-auth-plugin', or 'kubelogin' with token exchange args confirm exec-based rotation is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review CI/CD pipeline configuration and credential provisioning procedures to determine whether short-lived credential generation is enforced in the pipeline's kubeconfig bootstrapping step.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review CI/CD pipeline YAML (e.g., .github/workflows/, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile) for kubeconfig setup steps; look for aws eks update-kubeconfig, gcloud container clusters get-credentials, or equivalent commands that produce exec-plugin kubeconfigs vs. direct token injection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipelines using cloud CLI kubeconfig commands produce exec-plugin short-lived tokens; pipelines using kubectl config set-credentials with explicit tokens use static credentials.

typical_values: false (CI/CD pipelines using long-lived service account tokens)
true (managed clusters with OIDC or exec plugin)

option_description: Indicates whether kubeconfig files containing elevated credentials are stored in locations reachable by workload-zone actors — including Kubernetes Secrets in non-restricted namespaces (mountable by pods), CI/CD environment variables available to untrusted pipeline steps, shared NFS or network filesystem mounts, or developer workstations with network connectivity to cluster workloads.
security_impact: The Rego rule kubeconfig_credential_isolation_failure fires when this is true combined with elevated privilege level — in two distinct branches: (1) elevated/cluster_admin credentials + workload_accessible_storage + absent rotation, and (2) cluster_admin + workload_accessible_storage + any storage locations present. Workload-accessible storage means a compromised pod or malicious CI/CD job step can read the kubeconfig and use it to directly authenticate to the API server, crossing the workload-to-control-plane boundary via credential theft rather than vulnerability exploitation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search all Kubernetes Secrets across namespaces for kubeconfig content, identifying any stored in namespaces that lack strict RBAC isolation preventing pod mounting.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.data | to_entries[] | .value | @base64d | test("apiVersion: v1") and test("kind: Config")) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any results indicate kubeconfig stored as a Kubernetes Secret; evaluate the namespace's RBAC to determine workload mount accessibility.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check CI/CD system environment variables and pipeline secrets for kubeconfig data by examining pipeline configurations and secret references.
how_to_obtain.command: find . -name '*.yml' -o -name '*.yaml' -o -name 'Jenkinsfile' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -l -i 'kubeconfig\|KUBE_CONFIG\|kube_config' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files referencing kubeconfig in CI/CD pipeline definitions indicate potential workload-accessible storage if pipeline jobs are not strictly isolated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if the kubeconfig is mounted into any running pods via Kubernetes Secret volume mounts.
