how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]? | .secret? | .secretName? | test("kube|config|admin"; "i")) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, pod: .metadata.name, volume: [.spec.volumes[] | select(.secret?) | .secret.secretName]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any pods with kubeconfig-named secrets mounted indicate workload_accessible_storage = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview DevOps and platform engineering teams to identify shared filesystem paths (NFS, SMB, EFS) or shared developer machines where kubeconfig files with elevated credentials are placed and whether workload processes or untrusted CI jobs have read access to those paths.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review IAM policies, filesystem ACLs, and CI/CD job isolation boundaries; check whether pipeline jobs run in containers with access to secrets intended only for deployment steps.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Shared paths or insufficiently isolated CI/CD secret scopes confirm workload_accessible_storage = true.

typical_values: true (CI/CD pipelines with broad secret access)
false (dedicated operator workstations with strict access controls)

option_description: An enumerated list of all locations where kubeconfig files containing elevated credentials are stored across the environment — including CI/CD platform secret stores (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins), Kubernetes Secrets in various namespaces, developer workstations, shared network drives, version control repositories, and cloud secret managers. This inventory enables assessment of credential sprawl across trust zones.
security_impact: The Rego rule kubeconfig_credential_isolation_failure fires specifically when kubeconfig_privilege_level is 'cluster_admin', workload_accessible_storage is true, AND count(kubeconfig_storage_locations) > 0. A non-empty storage locations list combined with cluster_admin privilege and workload accessibility confirms that high-privilege credentials have spread to multiple locations, each representing an independent attack vector for crossing the workload-to-control-plane trust boundary. More storage locations exponentially increase the credential exposure surface.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search developer workstations and build agent paths for kubeconfig files, recording all discovered locations.
how_to_obtain.command: find / -name 'kubeconfig' -o -name 'config' -path '*/.kube/*' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -l 'kind: Config' 2>/dev/null; find /home /root /var/lib/jenkins /var/lib/gitlab-runner /opt -name '*.yaml' -o -name '*.yml' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -l 'current-context' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of filesystem paths where kubeconfig files exist; each path is a storage location entry.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query all Kubernetes Secrets across namespaces to find those containing kubeconfig data and record their namespace/name as storage locations.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}}/{{.metadata.name}} {{range $k,$v := .data}}{{$k}} {{end}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}' | grep -i 'kube\|config\|admin'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: namespace/secret-name entries represent Kubernetes Secret storage locations for kubeconfig data.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review CI/CD platform secret stores for kubeconfig entries stored as pipeline secrets or environment variables.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub Actions: Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions; GitLab: Settings > CI/CD > Variables; Jenkins: Manage Jenkins > Credentials > System; Azure DevOps: Pipelines > Library > Variable Groups — search for entries named KUBECONFIG, KUBE_CONFIG, or containing base64 kubeconfig data.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each CI/CD secret store containing kubeconfig data is recorded as a storage location (e.g., 'github_actions_secrets:KUBECONFIG').

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query cloud secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault) via API for secrets with kubeconfig-related naming conventions.
how_to_obtain.command: aws secretsmanager list-secrets --query 'SecretList[?contains(Name, `kube`) || contains(Name, `k8s`) || contains(Name, `cluster`)].{Name:Name,ARN:ARN}' --output table 2>/dev/null; vault kv list secret/ 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'kube\|k8s\|cluster'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secret names matching kubeconfig patterns in cloud secret managers are additional storage locations to record.

typical_values: ["~/.kube/config", "github_actions_secret:KUBECONFIG"]
["kubernetes_secret:ci-namespace/kubeconfig", "jenkins_credential:kube-admin"]

option_description: Indicates whether the Kubernetes API server has been started with a valid audit policy file referenced by the --audit-policy-file flag. Without this flag pointing to a non-empty policy file, all API server audit logging is disabled regardless of backend configuration, creating a complete blind spot for all control plane activity including secret access, privilege escalation, and lateral movement operations.
security_impact: The Rego rule control_plane_audit_log_blind_spot_in_lateral_movement_detection fires immediately when audit_policy_configured is false — this is the first and most fundamental check in the rule chain. Without any audit policy, there is no logging of any API server activity, meaning attackers can perform secret enumeration, exec into pods, bind elevated roles, or escalate privileges across the control plane boundary with zero audit trail. This makes detection of trust boundary crossings via legitimate-looking API calls impossible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the kube-apiserver process arguments directly on the control plane node to verify the --audit-policy-file flag is set.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o '\-\-audit-policy-file=[^ ]*' || kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].command}' | tr ',' '\n' | grep audit-policy
how_to_obtain.expected_output: --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml (or similar path) confirms the flag is set; absence confirms audit_policy_configured = false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Examine the kube-apiserver static pod manifest on the control plane node for the audit policy flag and verify the referenced file exists and is non-empty.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep -A2 'audit-policy' && cat $(cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep 'audit-policy-file' | awk -F'=' '{print $2}') 2>/dev/null | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Flag present in manifest and referenced file contains more than 0 lines confirms audit_policy_configured = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For managed Kubernetes clusters, query the cloud provider API or cluster configuration endpoint to determine if audit logging is enabled at the platform level.
how_to_obtain.command: aws eks describe-cluster --name <cluster-name> --query 'cluster.logging.clusterLogging[?enabled==`true`].types' 2>/dev/null; gcloud container clusters describe <cluster-name> --format='json' | jq '.loggingConfig' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Enabled log types including 'api' or 'audit' on managed clusters confirm audit policy is active at the platform level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for audit log output files on the control plane node as indirect evidence that an audit policy is configured and active.
how_to_obtain.command: ls -la $(cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml 2>/dev/null | grep 'audit-log-path' | awk -F'=' '{print $2}' | xargs dirname 2>/dev/null) 2>/dev/null || find /var/log -name '*audit*' -newer /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml 2>/dev/null | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of recently modified audit log files confirms an active audit policy; empty results suggest audit_policy_configured = false.

typical_values: false (self-managed clusters with default installation)
true (CIS-hardened clusters, managed EKS/GKE/AKS with audit enabled)

option_description: Classifies whether the API server audit policy includes RequestResponse-level logging for the specific sensitive verb combinations most critical for detecting lateral movement across control plane boundaries: get/list/watch on secrets, create on pods/exec and pods/attach subresources, and bind/escalate verbs on RBAC resources. 'full' means all categories are covered, 'partial' means some are covered, 'none' means none are configured at RequestResponse level.
security_impact: The Rego rule control_plane_audit_log_blind_spot_in_lateral_movement_detection fires when audit_policy_configured and audit_log_backend_enabled are both true but audit_policy_sensitive_verb_coverage is 'partial' or 'none'. This is the most nuanced condition — a cluster may have audit logging technically enabled but configured with an incomplete policy that omits exactly the verbs attackers use to cross trust boundaries: reading secrets to obtain credentials, exec-ing into pods for lateral movement, and binding elevated roles for privilege escalation. Partial coverage creates false confidence in detection capability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read the audit policy file and check for rules targeting secrets with get/list verbs, pods/exec and pods/attach subresources, and bind/escalate verbs on RBAC resources, all at RequestResponse level.
how_to_obtain.command: POLICY=$(cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep 'audit-policy-file' | awk -F'=' '{print $2}'); cat $POLICY | python3 -c "import sys,yaml; p=yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin); [print(r) for r in p.get('rules',[])]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules with level: RequestResponse covering resources: secrets (verbs: get,list), subresources: pods/exec (verbs: create), and RBAC resources with verbs: bind,escalate confirm full coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse the audit policy YAML to specifically check for the three critical coverage areas using jq or python, producing a structured gap analysis.
how_to_obtain.command:
python3 -c "
import yaml, sys
with open('/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml') as f:
    p = yaml.safe_load(f)
rules = p.get('rules', [])
rr_rules = [r for r in rules if r.get('level') == 'RequestResponse']
print('Secrets coverage:', any('secrets' in str(r.get('resources','')) for r in rr_rules))
print('Exec coverage:', any('pods/exec' in str(r.get('subresources','')) or 'pods/exec' in str(r.get('resources','')) for r in rr_rules))
print('RBAC escalate:', any('escalate' in str(r.get('verbs','')) or 'bind' in str(r.get('verbs','')) for r in rr_rules))
"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All three print statements showing True indicates full; one or two True indicates partial; all False indicates none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query existing audit logs to empirically verify whether sensitive verb events are being captured with request/response bodies, confirming effective coverage.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -h '' /var/log/kubernetes/audit/*.log 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "import sys,json; [print(json.loads(l).get('verb'), json.loads(l).get('objectRef',{}).get('resource'), json.loads(l).get('level')) for l in sys.stdin if any(v in l for v in ['secrets','exec','escalate','bind'])]" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Audit events for secrets/exec/bind/escalate at 'RequestResponse' level confirm coverage; events at 'Metadata' or 'Request' level only indicate incomplete coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For managed clusters, check the platform audit policy settings through the cloud provider console or API to understand what verb coverage the managed policy provides.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GKE: Console > Kubernetes Engine > Clusters > Logging & monitoring; EKS: Console > EKS > Clusters > Logging tab; check which log types are enabled and consult vendor documentation for which verbs are captured at RequestResponse level in the managed policy.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Vendor documentation or API response confirms which sensitive verbs are captured; many managed policies default to Metadata level for most events, yielding partial coverage.

typical_values: none (default minimal audit policies)
partial (CIS benchmark policies missing exec/escalate coverage)
full (purpose-built security-focused audit policies)

option_description: Indicates whether the API server has at least one functional audit log sink configured — either a file backend (--audit-log-path flag writing to a local file) or a webhook backend (--audit-webhook-config-file pointing to an external log aggregation endpoint). Without an active backend, audit events generated by the policy are silently discarded even if a policy file is configured.
security_impact: The Rego rule control_plane_audit_log_blind_spot_in_lateral_movement_detection fires in its second branch when audit_policy_configured is true but audit_log_backend_enabled is false. This represents a subtle but complete audit failure: the policy exists but events go nowhere, creating the illusion of audit coverage while producing no actual log records. Attackers crossing the control plane boundary through secret reads, exec sessions, or RBAC manipulation leave no trace, making the lateral movement detection gap functionally equivalent to having no audit policy at all.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the kube-apiserver manifest or process arguments for either --audit-log-path (file backend) or --audit-webhook-config-file (webhook backend) flags.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep -E '(audit-log-path|audit-webhook-config-file)' && ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -oE '\-\-(audit-log-path|audit-webhook-config-file)=[^ ]*'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Either --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log or --audit-webhook-config-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-webhook.yaml present confirms audit_log_backend_enabled = true; neither flag present means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the audit log file backend is actively writing by checking the file exists, is non-empty, and has been recently modified.
how_to_obtain.command: LOGPATH=$(cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml 2>/dev/null | grep 'audit-log-path' | awk -F'=' '{print $2}'); [ -f "$LOGPATH" ] && stat $LOGPATH && tail -1 $LOGPATH | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E '(stageTimestamp|requestURI)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File exists with recent modification time and valid JSON audit event in last line confirms file backend is active and writing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If a webhook backend is configured, verify the webhook config file exists and references a reachable endpoint.
how_to_obtain.command: WEBHOOK=$(cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml 2>/dev/null | grep 'audit-webhook-config-file' | awk -F'=' '{print $2}'); [ -f "$WEBHOOK" ] && cat $WEBHOOK | grep 'server:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Webhook config file present with a server URL confirms webhook backend is configured; test connectivity with curl to the endpoint URL.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For managed Kubernetes services, check the platform's audit log delivery configuration to confirm logs are being shipped to a storage backend.
how_to_obtain.command: aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix '/aws/eks' --query 'logGroups[*].logGroupName' 2>/dev/null; gcloud logging sinks list --filter='destination:*k8s*' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active log groups or sinks with recent write activity confirm the managed audit log backend is enabled and delivering events.

typical_values: false (newly provisioned clusters before hardening)
true (production clusters with file backend or SIEM webhook integration)

option_description: Indicates whether any pod running on a node has a hostPath volume mount referencing directories that contain kubelet PKI credentials or Kubernetes control plane certificates — specifically /var/lib/kubelet/pki, /var/lib/kubelet, /etc/kubernetes/pki, or /etc/kubernetes. Such mounts give container processes direct read access to the node's TLS client certificates used by the kubelet to authenticate to the API server.
security_impact: The Rego rule node_to_control_plane_impersonation_via_kubelet_credential_reuse fires unconditionally when kubelet_credential_host_path_mount_present is true — there is no qualifying condition that makes this acceptable. The second Rego branch also fires when this is true without node_restriction_admission_plugin_enabled. A pod with access to /var/lib/kubelet/pki can read the kubelet's client certificate and private key, then present those credentials to the API server to impersonate the node identity (system:node:<nodename>), which has permissions to read all secrets on that node's pods and modify node status — crossing the workload-to-control-plane boundary using the node's trusted identity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query all pod specs across all namespaces for hostPath volumes that reference kubelet or Kubernetes PKI directories.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | . as $pod | .spec.volumes[]? | select(.hostPath.path? | test("/var/lib/kubelet|/etc/kubernetes")) | [$pod.metadata.namespace, $pod.metadata.name, .name, .hostPath.path] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any output lines with kubelet or kubernetes pki paths confirm kubelet_credential_host_path_mount_present = true; no output confirms false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run a broader search including partial path matches and symlinked mounts that could indirectly expose PKI directories.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]? | .hostPath? | .path? | (startswith("/var/lib/kubelet") or startswith("/etc/kubernetes") or startswith("/var/lib/minikube") or startswith("/run/secrets/kubernetes.io"))) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, volumes: [.spec.volumes[] | select(.hostPath?) | {name: .name, path: .hostPath.path}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects listing pods with matching hostPath volumes; empty array confirms no such mounts exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check DaemonSets and privileged workloads specifically, as security tools, monitoring agents, and log collectors are the most common sources of this pattern.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get daemonsets --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | . as $ds | .spec.template.spec.volumes[]? | select(.hostPath.path? | test("/var/lib/kubelet|/etc/kubernetes")) | [$ds.metadata.namespace, $ds.metadata.name, .hostPath.path] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DaemonSet names and namespaces with matching paths; common findings include node-exporter, Falco, or custom log forwarders that may legitimately or mistakenly mount PKI paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Kubernetes API server directly with field selectors to efficiently scan pod specs without kubectl JSON parsing overhead in large clusters.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/pods?limit=500 | python3 -c "import sys,json; data=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(p['metadata']['namespace'], p['metadata']['name'], v['hostPath']['path']) for p in data['items'] for v in p.get('spec',{}).get('volumes',[]) if 'hostPath' in v and any(s in v['hostPath']['path'] for s in ['/var/lib/kubelet','/etc/kubernetes'])]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines with namespace, pod name, and path for any matching mounts; no output confirms kubelet_credential_host_path_mount_present = false.

typical_values: false (standard application workloads)
true (node monitoring DaemonSets, Falco, node-problem-detector, or misconfigured security tooling)

option_description: Controls whether kubelet client certificate and private key files stored at /var/lib/kubelet/pki/ are readable by non-root users. Specifically governs filesystem permission bits on kubelet-client-current.pem and related PEM files that contain node identity credentials used to authenticate to the API server.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires on node_to_control_plane_impersonation_via_kubelet_credential_reuse unconditionally when node_certificate_file_permissions_world_readable is true, and with increased severity when node_restriction_admission_plugin_enabled is also false. World-readable node certificates allow any process achieving execution on the node — including unprivileged container breakouts — to read the kubelet's private key and client certificate, then impersonate the node identity against the API server. Since the API server trusts node certificates as valid cluster principals, this crosses the workload-to-control-plane trust boundary using a legitimate credential without requiring any API server exploit.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check permission bits on all kubelet client certificate files across the PKI directory using stat. Look for mode 0644 or wider (world-readable) vs. the required 0600.
how_to_obtain.command: stat /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client*.pem
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure output shows 'Access: (0600/-rw-------)'. Any mode showing read bits for group or other (e.g., 0644) indicates true — world readable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use find to enumerate any kubelet PKI files with permissions wider than 0600 across all nodes. Run this on each node or via a daemonset/SSH loop.
how_to_obtain.command: find /var/lib/kubelet/pki/ -name '*.pem' -o -name '*.key' | xargs stat --format='%a %n' | awk '$1 > 600'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output means all files are 0600 or more restrictive (false). Any file listed indicates overly permissive permissions (true).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use ls -la to visually inspect permission flags on the entire PKI directory for both certificate and key files.
how_to_obtain.command: ls -la /var/lib/kubelet/pki/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files should show '-rw-------' (0600). If any show '-rw-r--r--' (0644) or wider, the attribute is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run a privileged DaemonSet across all nodes to audit certificate permissions cluster-wide and collect results via kubectl logs.
how_to_obtain.command:
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: cert-perm-audit
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cert-perm-audit
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cert-perm-audit
    spec:
      hostPID: true
      containers:
      - name: audit
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh","-c","stat /host/var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client*.pem && sleep 3600"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: pki
          mountPath: /host/var/lib/kubelet/pki
          readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: pki
        hostPath:
          path: /var/lib/kubelet/pki
EOF
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each node's pod logs will show stat output. Permissions of 0644 or wider on any node set the attribute to true for that node.

typical_values: false (hardened clusters with kubeadm defaults)
true (manually bootstrapped clusters or nodes where certificate rotation scripts reset permissions)

option_description: Controls whether the NodeRestriction admission controller plugin is active on the Kubernetes API server. When enabled, this plugin limits node identities (authenticated via node certificates) to only modifying their own Node object and only accessing Pod or Secret objects that are scheduled to that specific node, preventing nodes from reading arbitrary secrets or modifying other nodes.
security_impact: The Rego policy references node_restriction_admission_plugin_enabled as a mitigating control in node_to_control_plane_impersonation_via_kubelet_credential_reuse. Without NodeRestriction, a compromised node credential can read any Secret, modify any Node object, or access pod specs across the cluster — meaning stolen kubelet certificates from world-readable files yield full node-level API access cluster-wide. The policy fires with higher confidence when this is false alongside world-readable certificates, as the blast radius of credential reuse expands from node-scoped to cluster-scoped API access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the kube-apiserver static pod manifest on control plane nodes for the --enable-admission-plugins flag. This is the authoritative source for kubeadm-deployed clusters.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'NodeRestriction' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should contain 'NodeRestriction' within the --enable-admission-plugins value. Empty output means the plugin is absent (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the running kube-apiserver process arguments directly on the control plane node to confirm active configuration regardless of manifest.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o 'enable-admission-plugins=[^ ]*'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output like 'enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,...' confirms enabled (true). Missing NodeRestriction in the list means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use kubectl to retrieve the kube-apiserver pod spec from within the cluster and inspect admission plugin configuration.
how_to_obtain.command:
kubectl get pod kube-apiserver-$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].command}' | tr ',' '
' | grep admission
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Line containing '--enable-admission-plugins' should include 'NodeRestriction'. If absent, the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For non-kubeadm clusters using systemd service files, check the kubelet or apiserver service drop-in configuration for the admission plugin flags.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'NodeRestriction' /etc/systemd/system/kube-apiserver* /etc/kubernetes/ 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any match containing 'NodeRestriction' confirms the plugin is enabled (true). No output indicates it is not configured (false).

typical_values: true (kubeadm default since Kubernetes 1.14)
false (manually configured clusters, older deployments, or clusters using custom admission chains that omitted it)

option_description: Controls whether the ingress controller's service account is bound to a ClusterRole or ClusterRoleBinding that grants read access (get, list, watch) to Secret resources across all namespaces in the cluster. This is distinct from namespace-scoped access where the ingress controller can only read secrets within its own namespace.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires ingress_controller_privilege_escalation_to_control_plane when ingress_controller_cluster_scoped_secret_access is true alongside external traffic exposure and service account token automounting. This combination means an attacker who compromises the ingress controller (via a vulnerability in ingress processing, external request manipulation, or dependency exploitation) gains a service account token that can read every Secret in every namespace — including control plane certificates, database credentials, and API tokens stored as Secrets. The ingress controller's external exposure position makes this a high-value cross-zone escalation path from the internet to the control plane trust zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Find all ClusterRoleBindings whose subjects include the ingress controller service account name and examine the bound role for secrets access.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | (.kind=="ServiceAccount" and (.name | test("ingress"; "i")))) | {binding: .metadata.name, role: .roleRef.name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any ClusterRoleBinding output confirms cluster-scoped binding exists. Then inspect the referenced ClusterRole for secrets verbs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: After identifying the ClusterRole bound to the ingress service account, inspect it for secrets read permissions explicitly.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrole <ingress-clusterrole-name> -o jsonpath='{.rules[*]}' | python3 -c "import sys,json; rules=json.loads(sys.stdin.read() or '[]'); [print(r) for r in (rules if isinstance(rules,list) else [rules]) if 'secrets' in r.get('resources',[]) or '*' in r.get('resources',[])]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules output containing 'secrets' with verbs get/list/watch or '*' confirms true. Empty output means secrets are not in scope at cluster level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use kubectl auth can-i to directly test whether the ingress service account can read secrets cluster-wide, which confirms effective permissions including inherited rules.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl auth can-i get secrets --all-namespaces --as=system:serviceaccount:<ingress-namespace>:<ingress-sa-name>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'yes' means cluster-scoped secret access exists (true). 'no' means it does not (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API directly to list all ClusterRoleBindings and filter for the ingress controller service account subject.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | (.kind=="ServiceAccount" and (.name | test("ingress|nginx|traefik|contour|haproxy"; "i"))))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-empty JSON output with ClusterRoleBinding objects indicates cluster-scoped bindings are present. Review roleRef to confirm secrets are covered.

typical_values: true (NGINX ingress controller default Helm chart installs a ClusterRole with secrets access)
false (hardened installations using namespace-scoped roles only)
true (Traefik and Contour default configurations with cluster-wide IngressClass management)

option_description: Controls whether the ingress controller's RBAC permissions are exclusively delivered through RoleBindings scoped to its own namespace, with no ClusterRoleBindings granting cross-namespace or cluster-wide access. When enforced, the service account can only interact with Kubernetes API resources within its designated namespace.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires ingress_controller_privilege_escalation_to_control_plane when ingress_controller_namespace_isolation_enforced is false (not enforced) and the ingress controller is externally exposed with token automounting active. Namespace isolation being unenforced is the structural gap that allows the ingress controller's compromised service account to traverse from its deployment namespace into other tenant namespaces and cluster-level resources. This is the mirror condition to cluster_scoped_secret_access — absence of isolation enforcement means cluster-wide permissions are present by default in most ingress controller deployments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for the presence of any ClusterRoleBindings referencing the ingress controller service account. Any match means namespace isolation is NOT enforced.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | (.kind=="ServiceAccount" and (.namespace | test("ingress"; "i")))) | .metadata.name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty output (no ClusterRoleBindings found) suggests isolation may be enforced (true). Any binding name output means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that all RoleBindings for the ingress service account are confined to its own namespace only, with no cross-namespace references.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | (.kind=="ServiceAccount" and (.name | test("ingress"; "i")))) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, binding: .metadata.name, subject_namespace: .subjects[].namespace}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All subject_namespace values should match the ingress controller's own namespace. Cross-namespace RoleBindings indicate false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run a comprehensive RBAC summary for the ingress service account using kubectl-who-can or rbac-lookup tool to enumerate all permissions across namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl-who-can get secrets --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null | grep -i ingress || kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -A5 -B5 'ingress'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No cluster-wide secret access for ingress service accounts indicates true. Any cross-namespace access confirms false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the ingress controller Helm chart values or deployment manifests to confirm rbac.create is set and examine what role scope is configured in the chart templates.
how_to_obtain.command: helm get values <ingress-release-name> -n <ingress-namespace> | grep -i rbac; helm get manifest <ingress-release-name> -n <ingress-namespace> | grep -A20 'kind: ClusterRole'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of ClusterRole or ClusterRoleBinding in the manifest output confirms namespace isolation is enforced (true). Presence of ClusterRoleBinding means false.

typical_values: false (majority of default ingress controller installations use ClusterRoles)
true (custom hardened installations, GitOps-managed clusters with explicit RBAC scoping)
false (Helm chart defaults for nginx-ingress, ingress-nginx, and traefik)

option_description: Controls whether the Kubernetes Service fronting the ingress controller uses a type that accepts traffic from outside the cluster boundary, specifically LoadBalancer (which provisions an external cloud load balancer) or NodePort (which binds a port on every cluster node's external interface). ClusterIP services are not externally reachable without explicit port-forwarding.
security_impact: The Rego policy requires ingress_controller_exposed_to_external_traffic to be true as a necessary condition in both ingress_controller_privilege_escalation_to_control_plane firing conditions. External exposure places the ingress controller at the intersection of the external attack surface and the internal cluster trust zone. When combined with cluster-scoped RBAC and token automounting, external exposure means an internet-originating attacker who exploits any vulnerability in ingress request processing (SSRF, request smuggling, CVEs in the controller binary) immediately gains a service account with cross-namespace API server access, collapsing the layered trust boundary in a single exploit chain.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Service type for all services in the ingress controller namespace to identify LoadBalancer or NodePort types.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get svc -n <ingress-namespace> -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,TYPE:.spec.type,EXTERNAL-IP:.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip,PORT:.spec.ports[*].nodePort'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TYPE column showing 'LoadBalancer' or 'NodePort' means true. 'ClusterIP' means not directly externally exposed (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use jsonpath to extract only the service type field for the ingress controller service to get a clean true/false determination.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get svc -n <ingress-namespace> -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.type}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'LoadBalancer' or 'NodePort' in the output confirms external exposure (true). 'ClusterIP' only means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a TCP connection to the LoadBalancer external IP or any node IP on the NodePort from outside the cluster to confirm reachability.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -v --max-time 5 http://<external-ip-or-node-ip>:<port>/ -H 'Host: test.example.com'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any HTTP response (including 404 or 503) confirms the ingress is reachable externally (true). Connection refused or timeout suggests no external exposure (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API server for all services matching ingress-related labels across all namespaces to catch multi-namespace ingress deployments.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get svc --all-namespaces -l 'app.kubernetes.io/name in (ingress-nginx,traefik,contour,haproxy-ingress)' -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, ns: .metadata.namespace, type: .spec.type}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any item with 'type': 'LoadBalancer' or 'NodePort' confirms external exposure (true).

typical_values: true (production clusters where ingress is the intended internet entry point)
true (LoadBalancer type on cloud-managed Kubernetes: EKS, GKE, AKS)
false (development clusters using port-forwarding or internal ClusterIP only)

option_description: Controls whether Kubernetes automatically mounts a service account token into the ingress controller pod at the standard path /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. When automounting is active (default Kubernetes behavior), the JWT token is present in the pod filesystem and accessible to any process running inside the container with filesystem read access.
security_impact: The Rego policy includes ingress_controller_automount_service_account_token as a required true condition in both ingress_controller_privilege_escalation_to_control_plane firing rules. The token is the authentication credential that activates the RBAC permissions bound to the ingress controller's service account. Even if cluster-scoped RBAC exists, without the token being mounted in the pod the attacker cannot present it to the API server. When automounting is enabled, any code execution inside the ingress controller pod (via RCE in the controller, vulnerable backend, or supply chain attack) immediately yields a usable API server credential without requiring any additional privilege escalation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the automountServiceAccountToken field on the ingress controller Deployment spec. Absence of the field means it defaults to true.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get deployment <ingress-deployment-name> -n <ingress-namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.automountServiceAccountToken}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'true' or empty output (field absent, defaults to true) means automounting is active (attribute is true). 'false' means it is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the ServiceAccount object itself for automountServiceAccountToken, as this setting can be overridden at the ServiceAccount level and applies to all pods using that account.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get serviceaccount <ingress-sa-name> -n <ingress-namespace> -o jsonpath='{.automountServiceAccountToken}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'false' on the ServiceAccount disables automounting for all pods using it. Empty or 'true' means the default applies — check pod spec for override.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify whether the token file is actually present inside a running ingress controller pod, which is the ground truth for whether automounting is active.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <ingress-namespace> <ingress-pod-name> -- ls -la /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token 2>/dev/null && echo 'TOKEN_PRESENT' || echo 'TOKEN_ABSENT'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'TOKEN_PRESENT' confirms automounting is active (true). 'TOKEN_ABSENT' or exec error confirms the token is not mounted (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the ingress controller Helm chart values or deployment manifests in source control to check whether automountServiceAccountToken: false is explicitly set.
how_to_obtain.command: helm get manifest <ingress-release-name> -n <ingress-namespace> | grep -A2 -B2 'automountServiceAccountToken'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'automountServiceAccountToken: false' in the manifest means automounting is disabled (false). Absent field or 'true' confirms it is active (true).

typical_values: true (Kubernetes default — most ingress controller deployments do not override this)
false (CIS Benchmark-compliant hardened deployments where ingress controllers use projected volumes or external auth instead)
true (all major ingress controller Helm chart defaults including nginx-ingress and traefik)

option_description: Controls whether every tenant namespace in the cluster contains a default-deny NetworkPolicy covering both ingress and egress traffic. A default-deny policy ensures that all inter-pod and cross-namespace communication is denied unless explicitly permitted by additional NetworkPolicy rules, establishing a zero-trust baseline for namespace-level network segmentation.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires namespace_boundary_non_enforcement_in_multi_tenant_control_plane when default_network_policy_present is false. Without default-deny policies, any pod in any namespace can initiate connections to pods in other namespaces, including the kube-system namespace containing control plane components, admission webhook services, and monitoring infrastructure. In multi-tenant clusters, absence of default-deny allows a compromised tenant workload to reach API server endpoints, shared webhook services, and cross-tenant application pods, enabling trust zone traversal at the network layer even when RBAC restrictions are correct. The attribute must be true across ALL tenant namespaces to be considered enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all NetworkPolicies across all namespaces and identify which namespaces have a default-deny policy covering both ingress and egress directions.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector == {} and (.spec.policyTypes // [] | contains(["Ingress","Egress"]))) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Every tenant namespace should appear in the output with a default-deny policy. Missing namespaces indicate the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Get all non-system namespaces and cross-reference against namespaces that have any NetworkPolicy, identifying gaps where no policy exists at all.
how_to_obtain.command:
comm -23 <(kubectl get namespaces -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' | tr ' ' '
' | grep -v 'kube-system\|kube-public\|kube-node-lease' | sort) <(kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.namespace}' | tr ' ' '
' | sort -u)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty output means all non-system namespaces have at least one NetworkPolicy. Any namespace listed is unprotected — attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check a specific namespace for the presence of a correctly configured default-deny policy using kubectl describe to see policy details.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <tenant-namespace> -o yaml | grep -A10 'podSelector:\|policyTypes:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A default-deny policy has empty podSelector ({}) and policyTypes including both Ingress and Egress with no ingress/egress rules. Absence of such a policy means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the API server to count namespaces versus namespaces with default-deny policies to determine coverage ratio.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicies --all-namespaces -o json | jq '[.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector == {} and (.spec.policyTypes | contains(["Ingress","Egress"])))] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The count should equal the number of tenant namespaces. If count is less than the namespace count (minus system namespaces), the attribute is false.

typical_values: false (Kubernetes default — no NetworkPolicies are created automatically in new namespaces)
false (most managed Kubernetes services do not enforce default NetworkPolicies)
true (GitOps-managed clusters with namespace provisioning pipelines that apply default-deny templates)
true (clusters enforcing OPA/Gatekeeper policies requiring NetworkPolicy in every namespace)

option_description: Controls whether any ClusterRoleBindings or RoleBindings exist that grant service accounts originating in one tenant namespace access to resources in other tenant namespaces or cluster-wide control plane resources. This includes both explicit cross-namespace subject references in RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings that effectively elevate namespace-scoped service accounts to cluster scope.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires namespace_boundary_non_enforcement_in_multi_tenant_control_plane directly when cross_namespace_rbac_bindings_present is true. Cross-namespace RBAC bindings represent a logical trust boundary failure independent of network controls — even if NetworkPolicy prevents direct pod-to-pod communication, a service account with cross-namespace bindings can still traverse tenant boundaries via authenticated API server calls. A compromised pod in Tenant A namespace that inherits a ClusterRoleBinding to read Tenant B's secrets or modify cluster-level resources has bypassed multi-tenancy isolation entirely through legitimate API primitives, making this a high-fidelity indicator of control plane trust boundary weakness.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all ClusterRoleBindings where subjects are service accounts from tenant namespaces (non-system namespaces), which represent cluster-wide privilege grants.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | (.kind=="ServiceAccount" and (.namespace // "" | test("kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease") | not))) | {binding: .metadata.name, role: .roleRef.name, subjects: [.subjects[] | {sa: .name, ns: .namespace}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any non-empty output indicates ClusterRoleBindings for tenant service accounts exist (true). Empty output means no cross-namespace cluster bindings are present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Find RoleBindings in one namespace that reference service accounts from a different namespace, indicating cross-namespace role assignment.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | (.kind=="ServiceAccount" and .namespace != null and (.namespace != ""))) | select(.metadata.namespace != .subjects[0].namespace) | {binding_namespace: .metadata.namespace, binding: .metadata.name, subject_namespace: .subjects[0].namespace, sa: .subjects[0].name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any result shows a RoleBinding in one namespace granting access to a service account from another namespace (true).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use kubectl auth can-i impersonation to test whether service accounts from one tenant namespace can perform sensitive actions in another namespace.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n <other-tenant-namespace> --as=system:serviceaccount:<tenant-namespace>:<service-account-name>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'yes' confirms cross-namespace access exists for that service account (attribute is true). 'no' means the specific account lacks cross-namespace access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the cluster's RBAC configuration using rbac-lookup or rakkess tools to generate a complete permission matrix for all service accounts and identify cross-namespace grants.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl-who-can get secrets --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null | grep 'system:serviceaccount' | awk '{print $2}' | sort -u || rbac-lookup --kind ServiceAccount --output wide 2>/dev/null | grep -v 'kube-system\|kube-public'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service accounts appearing with access to namespaces other than their own, or with cluster-scope access, confirms true.

typical_values: false (well-governed clusters with automated RBAC review processes)
true (clusters that granted ingress or monitoring service accounts ClusterRoles for convenience)
true (multi-tenant clusters that use shared CI/CD service accounts with broad permissions)
false (clusters using hierarchical namespace controllers like HNC with strict RBAC isolation)
